handover.scope: Claude chat and Cowork · May 2026 snapshot
handover.title: Task completion and collaboration both remain common
handover.measure: Share of conversations classified as automation or augmentation; other conversations excluded.
handover.why: Shows how people use AI, not just whether they use it.
handover.credit: Redrawn from Anthropic's June 2026 data release. The provider classifies conversations as task completion (automation) or collaboration (augmentation). These labels do not show whether people checked AI's work.
handover.takeaway: In May 2026, 48.6% of classified Claude chat and Cowork conversations were labelled automation, versus 51.4% augmentation. Neither label tells us whether a person checked or acted on the output.

chart.aria: May 2026 Claude chat and Cowork: automation 48.62%, augmentation 51.38%, among conversations assigned either mode.

support.label: Bank of England / FCA: decision autonomy
support.text: A survey of UK finance distinguishes AI that automates part of a process from AI that acts fully independently. It remains unclear whether its percentages refer to firms or individual uses of AI. The finding remains provisional while this is reviewed, so no percentage is shown here.

notes: Coverage
Global Claude chat and Cowork, May 2026. Not all providers, workplace activity or Claude Code.
Definition
Automation: task completion, including feedback loops. Augmentation: learning, iteration or validation.
Data
Published bucket shares exclude the 2.61% labelled 'None', verified from component totals. The exclusion formula is not explicit in the documentation.
Limit
Company classification; actual review, use and reversibility of outputs are not observed. Sampling changes limit historical comparison.

related.title: How independently AI acts across products and tasks
related.text: The report uses an automated system to rate how independently AI acts in chat, Cowork and Claude Code. These exploratory ratings have not been validated as a measure of people losing control.

watch: How often people check, change or reject AI outputs.
Whether people can reverse decisions they hand over to AI, across providers and sectors.

work.scope: US payroll sample · Ages 22–25 · September 2026 release
work.title: Young-worker employment diverges by AI exposure
work.measure: Employment index by occupational exposure. Each group's November 2022 level = 100.
work.why: Tracks actual payroll outcomes for young workers, rather than predictions of which jobs AI could replace.
work.credit: All 60 monthly observations, September 2021–August 2026, from Stanford's dashboard. Exposure is not adoption; this comparison does not establish causation.
work.takeaway: From November 2022 to August 2026, employment among 22–25-year-olds fell 12.8% in the most AI-exposed fifth of occupations and rose 8.1% in the least exposed. This is a descriptive gap in the ADP sample, not a count of jobs lost to AI. In Denmark, workplaces encouraging chatbot use showed no extra decline in young workers' employment share through 2024.

support.label: Humlum & Vestergaard: Danish workplaces
support.text: Workplaces encouraging chatbot use showed no extra decline in the share of their workforce made up of young workers through 2024. The study covers a different country and period and measures a different outcome from the US comparison. It cannot rule out later US effects.

notes: Coverage
Ages 22–25 in a balanced sample of ADP client firms. Age is not career stage; the sample is not nationally representative.
Data
September 2026 release, all five exposure quintiles. Published index values; no averaging of groups or smoothing.
Limit
Exposure is not employer adoption. Education, earlier trends and other economic changes complicate attribution. No intervals supplied for these descriptive series.
Earlier headline
The paper's 19% shortfall pools different quintiles and ends in June 2026. It is not the endpoint of this chart.

related.title: The paper behind the dashboard
related.text: The paper describes the sample, other possible explanations, and an earlier comparison that combines exposure groups. Its roughly 19% shortfall measures how far employment fell below the level it would have reached if it had kept pace with the comparison group. That measure differs from the age-group comparison shown here.

watch: How hiring and training for junior workers change after employers adopt AI, with evidence of when adoption occurred.
Whether the employment gap persists across countries, samples and groups with different levels of education.

share.title: Labour's global income share is slightly lower
share.measure: Share of global GDP received as labour income, including estimated self-employed labour income.
share.why: An established international measure of how economic output is divided, with a baseline predating generative AI.
share.credit: Two values from ILOSTAT's March 2026 review show the start and end of the comparison. Both come from the same release. No values have been inferred for the years between them, so the chart does not show how the share changed each year.
share.takeaway: Labour's share of global GDP fell from 53.0% in 2015 to 52.6% in 2025: a 0.4-percentage-point decline. The ILO describes a partial recent recovery; these figures do not identify AI's contribution.

chart.axis: Labour income as a share of global GDP (%)
chart.aria: ILO global labour income share: 53.0% in 2015 and 52.6% in 2025. Zero to 100 percent scale.

support.label: BLS: US nonfarm-business labour share
support.text: The US nonfarm-business labour share was 52.8% in Q2 2026. It measures workers' compensation as a share of that sector's output. This series is updated more often, but its coverage and denominator differ from global GDP, so its value cannot be added to the ILO chart.

notes: Coverage
Global, including estimated labour income of the self-employed. Modelled estimates may be revised.
Data
2015 and 2025 values from one March 2026 publication. The live bulk download could not be retrieved, so no annual curve is shown.
Limit
Not typical wages, bargaining power or an AI effect. Countries and sectors can move in different directions.
Comparison
The BLS measure covers US nonfarm business. Its level cannot be directly compared with the global GDP measure.
watch: How workers' share of income changes within sectors and firms where AI adoption is documented.
Whether gains reach workers, including the self-employed, after accounting for other economic changes.

skills.scope: One Turkish high school · Randomized classroom trial · 2023
skills.title: The kind of AI help matters for later learning
skills.measure: Difference in exam scores without AI, compared with the no-AI group (adjusted estimates, in points out of 100).
skills.why: Tests what students can do after AI is removed, not just how well they perform with it.
skills.credit: The exam-score differences come from Table 1. Published estimates and standard errors are multiplied by 100 to express them in score points. Approximate 95% intervals are calculated as estimate plus or minus 1.96 times the standard error. Zero means no difference from the no-AI group.
skills.takeaway: After practice with unrestricted GPT, unaided exam scores were 5.4 points lower, about 17% relative to the no-AI group's mean. The guided tutor's −0.4-point estimate was not statistically distinguishable from no AI.

chart.aria: Adjusted unaided exam effects: unrestricted GPT Base minus 5.4 points; guided GPT Tutor minus 0.4 points. Approximate 95% intervals are minus 9.712 to minus 1.088 and minus 2.948 to plus 2.148. Zero is no difference from no AI.

support.label: The same trial: assisted performance
support.text: Both AI tools improved performance while students had access to them. That benefit did not translate into better exam scores when students were tested without AI.

notes: Coverage
One school, grades 9–11; short-term maths exams. Main model: 2,848 student-session observations, not unique students.
Chart data
Table 1 column 2 coefficients and standard errors × 100. Approximate intervals = estimate ± 1.96 × SE; calculated, not published endpoints.
−0.054 ÷ 0.321 ≈ −16.8%. The denominator is the no-AI mean. This is not a 17-point score difference.
Limit
Not permanent skill loss. Tutor's nonsignificant estimate does not prove equivalence. Guardrails and teacher guidance were bundled.

related.title: When people and AI work well together
related.publisher: Vaccaro, Almaatouq & Malone · Nature Human Behaviour, 2024
related.text: Across 106 experiments, people working with AI performed better on average than people working alone. Their average performance did not exceed that of whichever performed better on its own: people or AI. These experiments measure task performance. They do not show how well people retain their skills.

watch: Repeated tests of the same people without AI over months or years.
Which teaching and review practices preserve skills, and how quickly skills recover without AI.

culture.scope: One music platform · Figures dated August 2026
culture.title: AI music is a small share of recorded streams
culture.measure: Fully AI-generated tracks as a share of all recorded streams on Deezer.
culture.why: Streams are closer to consumption than upload counts, though fraudulent streams prevent a clean measure of human listening.
culture.credit: The range comes from Deezer's 13 October 2026 release and does not represent a confidence interval, which would describe statistical uncertainty. No 2% midpoint has been inferred. The period covered by the stream sample and any adjustment for fraud are unspecified.
culture.takeaway: Deezer reports AI-generated tracks at 1–3% of recorded streams, despite more than half of uploads being AI-made on peak days. Large supply does not establish large human attention, especially when streams can be fraudulent.
data: Fully AI-generated share of recorded streams

chart.aria: Fully AI-generated music accounts for a reported 1 to 3 of every 100 recorded streams on Deezer. Includes possible fraud; not a measure of human listening.

support.label: Deezer: more than 50% of uploads on peak days
support.text: Upload share measures the proportion of arriving tracks that are AI-generated. It does not count plays or listeners. The figure describes peak days and cannot be read as an average across days. It uses uploaded tracks as its total, while the chart uses recorded streams.

notes: Coverage
Deezer only; fully AI-generated tracks detected by the company's own tool, not all AI-assisted music.
Data
The release reports a 1–3% range. August 2026 date; sampling window unspecified. Squares show the range, not uncertainty around an estimate.
Limit
Streams may include fraudulent activity; adjustment is unspecified. Detected tracks are excluded from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists.
Transfer
Not an independent audit or a measure of culture-wide human influence.

related.title: Higher creativity ratings and more similar stories
related.text: In an experiment with 293 writers, access to AI-generated ideas was assigned at random. Access improved story ratings and made stories more similar to one another. This result from a limited experiment does not establish a trend across culture.

watch: Independent measurements of people's attention that exclude fraudulent activity.
Creators' income and the variety of creative work across platforms, alongside the amount of AI-generated content.

institutions.publisher: US Office of Management and Budget
institutions.scope: 2025 federal inventory · 3,611 individually reported use cases
institutions.gapNote: This inventory shows AI applications, not how much decision power has been delegated.
institutions.title: Government AI use is documented unevenly
institutions.measure: Number of individually reported AI use cases by development stage.
institutions.why: A public, reproducible starting point for finding systems that need decision-level monitoring.
institutions.credit: Counts come from the official CSV data file, using the version pinned to 14 May 2026. Entries with no development stage recorded remain a separate group. Agencies report these uses themselves; the counts do not provide an audit or show change over time.
institutions.takeaway: Of 3,611 reported use cases, 1,480 are explicitly marked deployed or pilot; 338 have no stage recorded. These counts show applications, not decisions, human reviews or successful appeals.

chart.axis: Number of individually reported use cases
chart.aria: 2025 federal AI inventory: 1040 deployed, 440 pilot, 1479 pre-deployment, 314 retired, and 338 with stage not reported. Total 3611.

support.label: OMB: inventory and field definitions
support.text: We still need comparable counts of decisions, meaningful reviews by people, cases where people overrule AI, and appeals. A blank field does not prove a safeguard is absent.

notes: Coverage
3,611 individual public use cases. Consolidated commercial-software reporting and exempt uses are outside this count.
Chart data
Counted every CSV row by development_stage; no imputation or deduplication. All five groups sum to 3,611.
Discrepancy
README says 1,818 deployed/piloted. Explicit CSV labels total 1,480; 338 blanks account for the difference. Kept separate pending review.
Limit
Reporting rules change. Counts do not measure decision volume, oversight quality or authority transferred.

related.title: From AI alerts to human action
related.text: The force reports 2,077 facial-recognition alerts, including 10 false alerts, over a year. Officers review alerts before acting. This is one force's report on its own system. It does not fully measure how often officers override alerts or provide an independent audit of bias.

watch: How many decisions AI systems with major consequences for people make, and how often people review those decisions carefully.
Whether people can challenge outcomes, and what happens after an appeal.

influence.gapNote: There is no validated overall measure here. Felt control is one contextual signal, not observed decision power.
influence.title: Most US adults feel little control over AI's use
influence.measure: Reported control over whether AI is used in their lives; share of US adults.
influence.why: A representative survey asks about people's experience of control directly, with published questions and methods.
influence.credit: Uses Pew's published response groups. The rounded percentages are reproduced without adjustment to their total. The original grouped chart omits the 1% who did not respond.
influence.takeaway: In June 2025, 57% of US adults said they had little or no control over whether AI was used in their lives. This measures felt control, not whether people have actually lost the ability to decide or appeal.
data: A great deal / quite a bit

chart.category: Felt control over whether AI is used
chart.aria: Pew June 2025: 57% of US adults report not too much or no control, 30% some control, and 13% a great deal or quite a bit. Rounded, nonresponse not shown.

rows.label: A great deal / quite a bit

support.label: Pew: 61% would like more control
support.text: The 61% comes from a separate question about wanting more control. It cannot be treated as the remaining share of the chart, which asks how much control people feel they have.

notes: Coverage
Representative US adult survey; June 2025. A dated snapshot, not a demonstrated decline.
Chart data
AICONTROL1, three groups published by Pew. The 1% nonresponse plus rounded categories totals 101%; values have not been rescaled.
Uncertainty
Full-sample margin of error: ±1.6 percentage points at 95% confidence. Not a category-specific interval.
Limit
Perceived control, not observed authority, political influence or AI-caused harm. Wanting more control is AICONTROL2.

related.title: Potential loss of control in AI conversations
related.text: A study by the AI provider flags a small minority of Claude conversations as potentially compromising people's beliefs, values or actions. These flags indicate possible risk; they do not confirm harm or a lasting loss of influence.

watch: Whether people can refuse, reverse or appeal decisions made with AI.
Link repeated surveys across countries to the choices people actually make and the outcomes they experience.
